Why Does Academic History Matter?

The study of history at UK universities appears to be under existential threat. Should anyone care?

The Lost History of the Aztec Empire

Before the Spanish conquest, the history of the Aztec Empire was recorded orally and with hieroglyphs. In danger of being lost or forgotten, Indigenous historians began to write it down.

Count Binface Should Read Bartolus

The jurisprudence of the Middle Ages may complement the legal efforts of today’s environmentalists.

The Decline of the Carolingians

The Carolingian Empire was consolidated by one of Europe’s most celebrated kings, but Charlemagne’s death meant that decline was inevitable.

Today’s featured articles

Behind the Times The Long Fight Against Deaf Exclusion

Speech, rather than hearing, has long been at the heart of deaf exclusion. Embracing sign language changed that.

Feature The Decline of the Carolingians

The Carolingian Empire was consolidated by one of Europe’s most celebrated kings, but Charlemagne’s death meant that decline was inevitable.

History Matters The Emancipation Proclamation Pocket Book

A miniature Emancipation Proclamation helped to recruit Black soldiers during the Civil War.

Months Past Death of Musical Coalman Thomas Britton

Coal merchant and concert promoter Thomas Britton passed away on 27 September 1714 after a prank went awry.

Making History Count Binface Should Read Bartolus

The jurisprudence of the Middle Ages may complement the legal efforts of today’s environmentalists.

Review ‘A History of the Novel in Britain’ by Philip Hensher review

Philip Hensher’s A History of the Novel in Britain is certainly novel but how does it fare as history?

Feature The 18th-Century Search for the Soul

Is the soul immortal, or does it die with the body? At the turn of the 18th century, amateur theologians like Henry Layton began to speculate, much to experts’ chagrin.

Head to Head Why Does Academic History Matter?

The study of history at UK universities appears to be under existential threat. Should anyone care?

Feature The FBI and the Nazi Spies

In 1938 a sensational spy trial exposed a Nazi plot to seduce and blackmail US officers. Despite America’s technological might, counterintelligence had been slow on the uptake.

Months Past The Hatry Group Collapse

Charles Hatry’s fraudulent business empire collapsed on 20 September 1929. It was the biggest crash the London stock market had ever seen.

Feature The Decline of the Carolingians

The Carolingian Empire was consolidated by one of Europe’s most celebrated kings, but Charlemagne’s death meant that decline was inevitable.

Image In the October 2026 issue:

Hirohito’s return to Europe, the lost history of the Aztec Empire, the decline of the medieval Carolingians, the FBI and the Nazi Spies, and the 18th-century search for the soul.

Plus: reviews, opinion, crossword, debate, and much more!

You can buy this issue from our website, from newsstands across the UK, or read it as a digital edition via the History Today App.

Wikiversity is a Wikimedia Foundation project for openly creating and sharing learning resources , collaborative learning projects , and research . It supports all levels and types of learning — from early childhood and school education to university study, professional development, and informal lifelong learning. Wikiversity is built by educators , students , researchers , and curious learners. Explore Wikiversity by taking a guided tour or jump in and learn how to add content and start editing . If you have any questions, join the main discussion in the Colloquium .

Multilingual Wikisource

The Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation announced on March 30 its decision to close all language editions of the project. In the announcement, a representative from Wikimedia Foundation cited motivations such as "long-term sustainability, levels of community activity, and the availability of reliable news coverage on other platforms". The announcement stated that all Wikinews editions—referring to the multiple language sections of Wikinews—would "transition to read-only mode" on May 4.

September’s featured text

That the reptiles were evolved from the Amphibia, and more specifically from that order known as the Temnospondyli, seems now assured. The earliest as also the most primitive reptiles that we know belong to the order called the Cotylosauria. With the exception of Eosauravus from the middle Pennsylvanian of Ohio, of which, unfortunately, the skull is unknown, our knowledge of them goes no further back than the late Carboniferous and early Permian. At that time there was a considerable diversity of known forms, belonging to at least four well-differentiated groups and twenty or more families; from which we may very properly conclude that their earliest ancestors, the beginning of their stock, lived much earlier, certainly at the beginning of the Upper Carboniferous, and very probably in Lower Carboniferous times. We therefore never can expect to find in the rocks of the Permian any real connecting link between the two classes.
